To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the "significance of human rights" comes from the "feeling toward violation of human dignity," which in turn comes from "mobilization of radical spheres of the public space" and from "intimacy of the household."

1) the concept of human rights has a genealogy that is not only related to political philosophy and the public sphere, but also to the intimacy of the domestic space, where it can be understood as an expression of the sentiment of fear; 2) the concept of fear has a genealogy which is not only related, in the public sphere, to the philosophical representation of terror, but also to fairy tales, where the "wolf" is a metaphor of unspeakable violence;
human rights are not just a matter of political theory and public discourse but they are also a matter of everyday life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between human rights and fear, as well as with the role of imagination and fantasy in the formation of human rights discourse.
the "private" genealogies of human rights, which can be traced back to the "domestic" space of the household.
the following questions: (i) What is the role of fear in the formation of human rights? (ii) How is fear conceptualized in political philosophy? (iii) How does fear appear in fairy tales?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the "wolf" is a metaphorical image that can help to understand how the violation of human human rights can be understood and narrated, and that this is possible only by linking private abuse to political terror.

, if human rights are a "feeling" of the violation, the "sense" and the "significance," which are the basis of human rights as political claims, are not to be searched only within the public sphere of the political community, but also within the private sphere of the family, where human rights are violated and where they can be imagined and narrated as a "fantastic" story.

the genealogy of human rights has to be read in a "private" perspective, in the sense that the "sense" that human rights make is not only the result of a juridification process, but also the result of the "sense of violation" that the human rights discourse has in the intimacy of daily life.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

human rights are the result of a "double" process: the juridification of public claims of validity, and the "translation" of private claims of validity into the public space, which is the result of the political mobilization of the private sphere.
the "wolf" is the metaphor of the "private" violation of the "public" human rights.
human rights discourse is a public and private matter, and that the private dimension of human rights is a matter of life and death for women and children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the private sphere is the place where human rights violations are most often committed, and the most effective way of preventing such abuses is by raising public awareness of them.
human rights cannot be understood as a mere juridical construction. Rather, they have to be seen as the result of an "affective" and "aesthetic" process of public justification.

, if we are to understand the significance of human rights as something that is not merely the product of the juridical-political discourse, then the "significance of human rights" must be sought in the "significance attributed to the human" in private life.
